title: Does Teaching a Lesson Make You Brave?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a line from Daniel Nayeri's memoir Everything Sad Is Untrue about creation as an act of bravery, Stuart reflects on late-winter teacher fatigue and argues that persisting in the work of lesson-making under weariness is itself a form of quiet courage. He describes the cumulative labor, mental, spiritual, and emotional, of seven or eight months into the school year, and the tension between illusory limiting beliefs and real, rock-solid limits. Drawing on Nayeri's grandmother, who created poems despite heartbreak and brutality, Stuart argues that hardship doesn't cancel out beauty; it can actually deepen it, making ordinary acts of teaching more remarkable rather than less. He closes by widening the lens to classrooms all around the world where fatigued or disheartened teachers are nonetheless making an honest attempt at education, calling that a quietly beautiful, even startling, thing to behold.
points: Stuart uses Daniel Nayeri's line, that making anything is a brave thing to do in a hard world, to reframe ordinary lesson planning during a fatiguing stretch of the year as an act of courage, not just routine.
He distinguishes between illusory limits that can be pushed past and real limits that can't, a useful filter for late-year burnout.

The argument inverts the usual framing of hardship: the more difficult the season, the more an honest effort at teaching takes on the qualities of beauty and bravery, rather than simply being a grind to survive.

The piece ends by widening the frame from one teacher's fatigue to a global picture of weary teachers still showing up — a reminder that this kind of quiet persistence is happening in classrooms everywhere, not just one's own.
quotes: I think what's hardest this time of year is that you're carrying around with you this weight of all the weeks and all the days. It's been labor: mental, spiritual, emotional.

It's been the labor of discovering once again that there are limits to what you can do but that these limits don't permit you to give up because some of them are illusory, hallucinations of our limiting beliefs. But then, other limits are as real as rocks.
But this is the weird thing about hardship: the more you experience it, the more your acts of creation take on the qualities of beauty and bravery.

And so to create a lesson, an honest effort at helping a group of young people to get better at something…doing that when under the weight of fatigue or weariness or ennui, that is a remarkable and beautiful thing.
All around the world, in all kinds of schools, there are fatigued or weary or disheartened teachers who are, in the face of these feelings, nonetheless making a true attempt at education today.
